claim_verdicts.evidence: how-query-works.md, "When queries are executed": "When you call LINQ operators, you're simply building up an in-memory representation of the query. The query is only sent to the database when the results are consumed." Listed triggers: "Iterating the results in a `for` loop"; "Using an operator such as `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Single`, `Count`, or the equivalent async overloads" - ToListAsync/FirstOrDefaultAsync are such async overloads. EF Core 10 whatsnew/breaking-changes list no change to execution timing.

how-query-works.md, "The life of a query": "The database provider identifies which parts of the query can be evaluated in the database / These parts ... are translated to database-specific query language (for example, SQL...) / A query is sent to the database and the result set returned". That page carries an "out of date" banner, so also settled by execution: ToQueryString() on the lesson's own chain (EF Core 10 + Npgsql, stage-1 DbContext) printed one statement: SELECT ... FROM orders AS o INNER JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.customer_id = 1 ORDER BY o.id.
claim_verdicts.source: refs/efcore-docs/.../how-query-works.md; dotnet run against DonHang.Infrastructure @ stage-1, 2026-09-24

claim_verdicts.evidence: single-split-queries.md: "When working against relational databases, EF loads related entities by introducing JOINs into a single query" and "EF Core uses single query mode by default in the absence of any configuration." DonHangDbContext @ stage-1 configures no splitting behaviour. Confirmed by ToQueryString(): Include(o => o.Customer) -> one statement with "INNER JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.id"; Include(o => o.Items) -> one statement with "LEFT JOIN order_items AS o0 ON o.id = o0.order_id". No second statement in either case.

`git -C examples/don-hang show stage-1:DonHang.Infrastructure/EfOrderRepository.cs` is 19 lines and byte-identical to the lesson's block (lines 1-19). Both query methods are expression-bodied and neither uses async/await: "public Task<Order?> FindAsync(int id) => db.Orders.Include(o => o.Items).FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id);" and "public Task<List<Order>> ListByCustomerAsync(int customerId) => db.Orders.Where(...).Include(...).OrderBy(...).ToListAsync();". Claim correctly scoped to those two; AddAsync in the same file does use async/await (section-5 issue).

Live run 2026-09-24 against the stage-1 lab (localhost:8080). anh.tran@example.com -> ids 1 (paid), 2 (shipped), 10 (paid), all customerName "Trần Minh Anh"; chau.nguyen@example.com -> ids 3 (paid), 4 (cancelled), 11 (shipped), all "Nguyễn Bảo Châu" — disjoint id sets, no overlap. OrdersController.List() @ stage-1 reads customerId from the token's `sub` claim and calls repository.ListByCustomerAsync(customerId), so both responses come from the same code path.
claim_verdicts.source: curl POST /api/v1/auth/login + GET /api/v1/orders, both accounts; DonHang.Api/Controllers/OrdersController.cs @ stage-1

issues.text: False about the statement EF Core actually sends. ToQueryString() on this lesson's own chain (EF Core 10, Npgsql, DonHangDbContext @ stage-1) prints: "SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, ... FROM orders AS o INNER JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.customer_id = 1 ORDER BY o.id". The WHERE sits in the middle; the statement ends in ORDER BY o.id, because ListByCustomerAsync also chains .OrderBy(o => o.Id) — which the lesson itself stresses two sections earlier.
issues.quote: it ends in `WHERE customer_id = ...`, so other customers' rows never leave the database at all
issues.fix: Write "it carries a `WHERE customer_id = ...` (with the `ORDER BY` from `.OrderBy(...)` after it), so other customers' rows never leave the database at all". Apply the same correction to quiz q6's explanation for option c, en and vi (see the q6 issue).

issues.text: Unlisted claim: the lesson's only observable evidence is now a C# type claim — that `var query = db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == customerId)` has declared type `IQueryable<Order>`, not `List<Order>` — stated four times (sections 2, 4, 6 second bullet, summary line 5), and no claim in .meta.json covers it. It is true (a generic probe `static string StaticTypeOf<T>(T _)` applied to that exact expression, compiled against DonHang.Infrastructure @ stage-1 with SDK 10.0.300, printed System.Linq.IQueryable'1[DonHang.Domain.Order]), but the ledger hides that the whole lesson now rests on it.

issues.text: Contradicted by the code block printed six lines above it: "public async Task AddAsync(Order order) => await db.Orders.AddAsync(order);" is one of the methods "here", and it writes both `async` and `await`. As stated, the sentence tells the reader that a line visible on the same page does not exist. (Ledger claim 4 is correctly scoped to FindAsync/ListByCustomerAsync; the prose generalises past it.)
issues.quote: Each method here is a single expression, so the chain's own `Task` is what gets returned directly, with no `async`/`await` written.
issues.fix: Cut the sentence (it teaches a C# idiom outside this lesson's outline), or scope it to the two query methods: "Neither query method writes `async`/`await` — each is one expression, so the chain's own `Task` is returned directly."

issues.text: Overstated: a compile-time type cannot say whether rows were fetched. `new[] { order }.AsQueryable()` is also an `IQueryable<Order>` and its rows are already in memory. What the type shows is that the call handed back a query object rather than a materialised result; it is EF Core's deferred execution — "The query is only sent to the database when the results are consumed" — that guarantees nothing ran. The type is a sign of it, not the proof.
issues.quote: its declared type already says no rows have been fetched; nothing runs until something enumerates it
issues.fix: Write "its declared type shows `.Where(...)` handed back a query, not a result — and an EF Core query is not sent to PostgreSQL until something enumerates it".

issues.text: "right up until" implies the variable changes type once `.ToListAsync()` runs. It does not: the variable stays `IQueryable<Order>`; `.ToListAsync()` returns a separate new `List<Order>`. Confirmed by the compile check — the queryable variable's static type is IQueryable<Order> both before and after that call.
issues.quote: has type `IQueryable<Order>`, not `List<Order>`, right up until `.ToListAsync()` is called on it
issues.fix: Write "...has type `IQueryable<Order>`, not `List<Order>`; the `List<Order>` only ever appears as what `.ToListAsync()` hands back".

issues.text: Not the same kind of object. `db.Orders` is a `DbSet<Order>` (DonHangDbContext: `public DbSet<Order> Orders => Set<Order>();`); `.Where(...)` returns an `IQueryable<Order>`, verified by compile check. `DbSet<Order>` implements `IQueryable<Order>`, not the reverse — so the chaining works, but the result is not a DbSet and does not carry DbSet members such as `AddAsync`, which this same lesson shows being called on `db.Orders`.
issues.quote: That queryable is the same kind of object `db.Orders` itself is, so further calls chain onto it the same way.
issues.fix: Write "`db.Orders` is itself one of these queryables, so further calls chain onto the result the same way they chain onto `db.Orders`".

issues.text: Reads as an exhaustive list because of "only ... does that". The documentation lists more enumerating operators: "Using an operator such as `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Single`, `Count`, or the equivalent async overloads" — so `.ToArrayAsync()`, `.SingleAsync()`, `.CountAsync()` and others also send the query. The lesson's three are examples, as Core concepts correctly presents them.
issues.quote: only `.ToListAsync()` — or `.FirstOrDefaultAsync()`, or a `foreach` over the query — does that
issues.fix: Write "only a call that asks for results does that — `.ToListAsync()`, `.FirstOrDefaultAsync()`, a `foreach` over the query", dropping the closed-list reading.
